newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Aid workers shocked by empty refugee camp in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Aid workers shocked by empty refugee camp in Zaire.

text.p: Foreign aid workers said they would keep pressing for access to 55,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees, many too weak and sick to walk, who disappeared from a refugee camp in rebel territory.
Aid workers said they were shocked to see Kasese camp, 25 km (15 miles) south of Kisangani, empty on Thursday.
They found not a single refugee dead or alive at the camp, which had 55,000 residents and had been sealed off to aid workers on Monday.
"My impression was that the place was extremely sanitary for a camp where people had fled at a moment's notice," said Brenda Barton, a spokeswoman for the U.N. World Food Programme (WFP).
The U.N. refugee agency UNHCR said it was the first time a large group of Hutu refugees disappeared in rebel territory and the rebels was responsible for explaining what had happened.

UNHCR spokesman Paul Stromberg said he had a list of 9,000 extremely vulnerable people among the 55,000 who were in no condition to walk. "I don't know how many of these cannot walk but there were 9,000 who shouldn't walk," he told Reuters.
A Zairean farmer from nearby Kasese village told reporters watched by rebel guards that refugees killed six villagers on Monday and on Tuesday "we went to discuss with the refugees".
"They started attacking us," said Merindo Masoudi. Asked where they were, he said: "They fled because they did wrong... There may have been some refugees killed but it was those who did wrong."
A camp cholera hospital, which had about 300 very sick patients, stood abandoned with bags for intravenous drips hanging from bamboo walls. The tents at the hospital had gone.
Overall there was very little debris when compared with other camps abandoned by the refugees in their six-month exodus.
The U.N. Security Council on Thursday harshly criticised the rebels for preventing aid from reaching up to 100,000 refugees south of Kisangani and obstructing their return home to Rwanda.
The council called "in the strongest terms" on the rebels "to ensure unrestricted and safe access by all humanitarian relief agencies" and said it was alarmed by reports of massacres in east Zaire.
It said rebels should allow U.N. investigators to inspect certain sites, but it was unclear if these included Kasese.
Rebels have seized more than half of Zaire since October and say Kinshasa is in their sights.
The Tutsi-dominated rebels sealed off the Kasese and Biaro camps south of Kisangani from aid workers and journalists on Monday, saying they were conducting a military operation.
The Hutus fled Rwanda in 1994 and are collectively accused by minority Tutsis of genocide in Rwanda in the same year.
Rebels agreed to allow the U.N. mission to Kasese only after U.N. chief Kofi Annan said he was appalled by the "inhumanity" of their action which was killing the refugees by starvation.
Aid workers had feared that many of the 80,000 Rwandan refugees south of Kisangani had fled because of fighting in the area on Tuesday between rebels, local villagers and refugees.
Zairean villagers said on Wednesday Tutsi-dominated rebels had killed hundreds of Rwandan Hutu refugees at Kasese and a battle between rebels and refugees accompanied the slaughter.

"The Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire...does not have a policy which consists in making life more difficult for the refugees," said Raphael N'genda, "information minister" in rebel-held Lubumbashi on Thursday.
He said France should let ailing Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko use a supersonic Concorde airliner if he is too sick as he says to take a normal flight to talks in South Africa.
U.N. special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun was expected in South Africa to settle a date for talks between the warring parties in Zaire, South African Deputy Foreign Minister Aziz Pahad said.
But Pahad said in Cape Town there was no viable proposal on the table as Mobutu said he was too ill to reach South Africa.
The rebels said on Wednesday they had captured three gateway towns to Kinshasa and military analysts said guerrillas were in a position to choke off much of the capital's vital supplies.
